newsitem.title: EGYPT: Israel's Levy to Egypt to see Mubarak, Moussa.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Levy to Egypt to see Mubarak, Moussa.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak will hold talks with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy in Cairo on Tuesday on the growing crisis in Middle East peace efforts, officials said on Monday.
Palestinian-Israeli peace talks were thrown into further jeopardy by a double suicide bombing in a west Jerusalem market on Wednesday in which 13 people were killed and 170 were wounded.
Palestinians asked for an Arab League extraordinary meeting of permanent representatives which will take place on Tuesday to assess the situation.

Foreign Minister Amr Moussa told reporters he would also meet Levy to discuss "the current circumstances of the peace process and the difficulties it faces, whether from the security angle or other measures that have obstructed the peace process and led to its freeze over the past few months."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the right-wing Likud bloc, told his cabinet on Sunday that Israel would not honour peace deals it signed with Yasser Arafat unless the Palestinian leader cracked down on Moslem militants behind the bombing.

Israel also suspended peace talks with the Palestinians, rounded up scores of suspected militants, closed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, demanded the extradition of the PLO police chief and threatened to re-enter Palestinian self-rule areas to seize militants if Arafat failed to do the job.

The Palestinians say Israel's failure to implement past peace deals, including the release of thousands of Palestinian prisoners and its proceeding in building Jewish settlements in the heart of Arab East Jerusalem, led to the current crisis.

Egypt, which became the first Arab state to make peace with Israel in 1979, has been trying to revive Israeli-Palestinian peace talks which collapsed when Israel broke ground on a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem in March.
Asked if contacts Egypt had launched with the Palestinians and the United States would lead to a breakthrough, Moussa said:
"This depends on what the two sides (Israel and the Palestinians) can offer within the framework of precise implementation of their obligations according to the Oslo (peace) accord.
"The two sides must undertake this implementation and make progress according to what has been agreed upon and with an eye on maintaining calm, security and restraint," Moussa said.

Al-Ahram government daily newspaper said in its Monday edition that Moussa and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright discussed by telephone "developments in the dangerous situation through which the peace process is passing" and the forthcoming visit to the region by U.S. envoy Dennis Ross.
The paper, quoting diplomatic sources, said Albright "promised to do all she could to save the peace process and affirmed her distress at the security situation".
Moussa told Albright that U.S. efforts to revive the peace talks must take into account, alongside the security angle, the other problems faced by the peace process, al-Ahram said.
Arafat said during his visit to Egypt on Saturday that U.S. President Bill Clinton must intervene to resolve the crisis.
Clinton has said he would send Ross to the region once the mourning in Israel was over and that any visit by Albright to the Middle East would only take place after Ross's visit.
